entries.title: E INK invests in Soofa, a provider of solar-powered digital information kiosks
entries.summary: Financial terms of the investment, including the amount invested and E Ink’s ownership stake in Soofa, were not disclosed. The post E INK invests in Soofa, a provider of solar-powered digital information kiosks first appeared on Good e-Reader.
entries.content:
E INK has just announced a strategic investment and partnership with Soofa, a provider of solar-powered digital information kiosks, to accelerate the deployment of sustainable outdoor signage across U.S. communities. The investment will support Soofa’s expansion and the adoption of E Ink’s 75-inch Kaleido Outdoor color ePaper displays, which are designed to deliver readable digital content in direct sunlight while consuming significantly less electricity than conventional digital signage.

Founded in 2014, Soofa develops solar-powered kiosks that display local news, public transportation updates, weather information, community announcements, and advertising in public spaces. The company has established relationships with more than 60 U.S. cities, including Boston, Atlanta, and Los Angeles. Its kiosks are designed to operate without connections to conventional electrical infrastructure, allowing municipalities, property owners, and advertisers to install digital information displays in locations where wired power may be difficult or expensive to provide.

Soofa’s kiosks are also designed for relatively straightforward installation. According to the companies, a two-person team can install the units without specialized equipment, reducing some of the logistical requirements associated with conventional digital signage.

“Soofa shows how E Ink technology can make useful information more accessible while keeping energy consumption low,” said Johnson Lee, chairman and CEO of E Ink.

“Our shared MIT Media Lab roots and longstanding collaboration make this investment especially meaningful. We are pleased to support Soofa’s next stage of growth and help bring sustainable community signage to more neighborhoods.”

The investment is part of E Ink’s broader strategy of supporting companies developing commercial applications for its display technology.

The Soofa transaction represents E Ink’s first investment in a company offering a complete digital signage solution, extending its involvement beyond display components into a business that combines hardware deployment, advertising operations and community relationships. The partnership brings together E Ink’s display development and manufacturing capabilities with Soofa’s experience operating public-facing advertising and information networks.

The investment positions Soofa to expand its solar-powered signage network while giving E Ink a more direct role in the growing market for low-power outdoor digital displays and community advertising infrastructure.

entries.title: Will you buy the new iPad Mini to read comics or books?
entries.summary: Would you buy the new Apple iPad Mini with an OLED screen to read books, comics, manga, magazines, or digital newspapers? The post Will you buy the new iPad Mini to read comics or books? first appeared on Good e-Reader.
entries.content:
The newly released 8th-generation Apple iPad mini is powered by the A20 Pro chip and went on sale on November 6, 2026. This marks the most significant redesign in the device’s history, shifting to a stunning 8.5-inch Super Retina XDR OLED display while trimming its thickness to just 5.4 mm.

The 8th-generation iPad mini (2026) is a major leap forward for Apple’s smallest tablet, defined by its stunning 8.5-inch Super Retina XDR OLED display and ultra-thin 5.4 mm chassis. The shift to OLED completely transforms the visual experience, delivering deep contrast, 1,200 nits of peak HDR brightness, and a 24% reduction in bezel size that makes the hardware feel incredibly modern. Under the hood, the A20 Pro chip combined with 12GB of RAM turns this compact device into an absolute powerhouse, making multitasking fluid and driving local Apple Intelligence features with ease.

However, the redesign introduces a few bold engineering choices that serve as distinct trade-offs. To secure its new IP67 water and dust resistance rating, Apple eliminated physical speaker grilles entirely in favor of an Acoustic Display system that vibrates the screen to emit sound. While this projects audio directly toward the viewer, it can cause a noticeable physical vibration against your fingers at high volumes and lacks the acoustic depth of dedicated speaker ports. Furthermore, despite the premium price hike and the gorgeous OLED panel, the screen remains locked at a 60Hz refresh rate, which may disappoint users accustomed to the buttery-smooth scrolling of ProMotion on iPad Pro or iPhone Pro models.

If your primary use case is reading, investing an extra $150 for the matte nano-texture glass finish (available on the 256GB and 512GB tiers) is highly recommended. It scatters ambient light to drastically eliminate harsh reflections and mimics the glare-free properties of an E Ink e-reader, allowing you to comfortably read text outside or under bright overhead lights. Reading Comics, manga, magazines, newspapers, or e-books should provide a really good experience. Many app developers see the iPad as their flagship platform, so it gets lots of new features and enhancements before the Android version does. If you use the Kindle or Kobo app on the iPad, you can purchase digital content in the app.

Would you buy the new iPad Mini to read books and other content? The new device is more portable, weighs less and makes it easier to read on the go.

entries.title: Everything you want to know about Kobo Stack
entries.summary: Stack is the only option that makes a sideloaded book behave like a store-bought one, with progress and annotations syncing across devices. The post Everything you want to know about Kobo Stack first appeared on Good e-Reader.
entries.content:
Send to Kobo was officially announced last week, and the system is live on the Kobo Beta, currently available on their latest-generation e-readers. A Kobo Stack subscription is needed to take advantage of this feature. You can also use Send to Kobo by email, drag-and-drop upload e-books on kobo.com, sync your uploaded books and their annotations across devices, and use the extra journal and note-taking workbooks.

Here is how the Kobo Stack works. Email your e-books (PDF, EPUB, and LCP EPUB) and documents to your unique Kobo Stack address. They’ll instantly appear in your library on any connected device, such as e-readers or Kobo apps. Drag and drop EPUB and PDF files using the upload tool in the Kobo Cloud on the main Kobo website. A subscription also supports Libby with multiple library cards, but the free tier allows this too. If you have a Libra Color, you can sync uploaded content & annotations across devices and use exclusive journaling and note-taking workbooks.

Kobo Stack subscription provides three years of worry-free reading. The extended manufacturer’s warranty offers comprehensive protection for your Kobo e-reader, instead of the default one-year warranty.

If you stop paying for the Kobo Stack subscription, you get a 60-day grace period. After that, the notes and annotations stored in Stack are permanently deleted, and so is anything else living only in the Stack cloud. Books already on your device stay, and so do your Kobo purchases. Kobo itself tells you to export your notes and download your files during those 60 days.

Stack needs the Kobo OS 6 beta, so for now it is limited to the Kobo Libra Colour, Kobo Clara Colour and Kobo Clara BW. The subscription costs around $3.99 USD per month, and the service costs around €2.99 per month. A free 90-day trial is available for beta participants. It remains to be seen whether the free trial will remain available once it rolls out to all Kobo users, or whether they will shorten the free subscription tier.

Some things you don’t need a Stack subscription for. You can use multiple library cards from Libby-supported libraries in your country. Users can load books onto their Kobo e-reader by simply using a USB cable. Calibre: great if you already keep a library on a computer. Wireless transfer is possible, but it requires your computer to be on and some setup. Dropbox or Google Drive access is still free for modern Kobo e-readers.

To subscribe to Stack, click this link and log in to your Kobo account with your username and password. The subscription uses your preferred payment method that is attached to your account and is charged every month after the trial is ended.

entries.title: First Look at the Pocketbook INKPAD EO 2
entries.summary: The PocketBook InkPad Eo 2 is a premium 10.3-inch color e-note designed for reading, writing, and digital note-taking. The post First Look at the Pocketbook INKPAD EO 2 first appeared on Good e-Reader.
entries.content:
The PocketBook InkPad Eo 2 is a high-end, 10.3-inch color e-note and e-reader tablet running on Android 14. Launched in September, this second-generation device focuses heavily on productivity, combining a vibrant color display with an open app ecosystem and advanced handwriting recognition. However, it is still not available to be purchased yet on Amazon.

The PocketBook InkPad Eo 2 is a 10.3-inch color e-note tablet that features an E Ink Kaleido 3 display, offering a sharp 300 DPI for grayscale content (1860 x 2480) and 150 DPI for its 4,096-color mode (930 x 1240). Running on an open Android 14 operating system with full access to the Google Play Store, the device is powered by an octa-core MediaTek MT6765 processor clocked at 2.3GHz, paired with 4GB of RAM and 64GB of internal storage, which can be expanded via a microSD slot. To ensure visibility in any environment, it incorporates a SMARTlight frontlight system that lets users adjust both screen brightness and color temperature.

For productivity and multimedia, the 470-gram tablet has a large 4900 mAh battery and a proprietary active digital stylus (the PocketBook Stylus 2) for AI-powered handwriting recognition. Audio capabilities are highly integrated, featuring built-in stereo speakers and a quad-microphone array alongside Bluetooth 5.0 and Wi-Fi connectivity for seamless audiobook playback and voice recording. Physically, the device measures 191 x 225.6 x 7 mm, houses a USB-C port for charging and data transfer, and showcases a distinct, premium pinstriped backplate design.

Pocketbook’s strength is the number of supported e-book formats in its stock e-reading app. It supports AZW, AZW3, DOC, DOCX, EPUB, FB2, FB2.ZIP, HTM, HTML, MOBI, PDF, PRC, RTF, and TXT. Google Play will ensure you can install 3rd party apps on it, such as Libby, or Kindle.

entries.title: Will you buy the Pocketbook Q e-reader?
entries.summary: The PocketBook Q is an excellent, distraction-free pocket e-reader featuring a crisp 300 PPI display and tactile page-turn buttons, though its Linux system means you miss out on third-party Android apps like Kindle. The post Will you buy the Pocketbook Q e-reader? first appeared on Good e-Reader.
entries.content:
The PocketBook Q is a compact, smartphone-sized e-reader designed specifically for one-handed reading and “digital detox”. It debuted at the IFA 2026 trade show in Berlin and is launching across retail markets in late November. This device is similar to the BOOX Picco.

The Pocketbook Q features a 5.84’’ touchscreen display with an E INK Carta 1300 e-paper panel. The resolution is 788 × 1576 at 300 PPI, and it has a black-and-white display. Adaptive SMARTlight lets readers adjust both brightness and color temperature, shifting from crisp, cooler tones during the day to warmer ones for evening reading. With the LEDs illuminating the screen rather than shining directly into the eyes, reading stays comfortable even in total darkness. Dark Mode offers even more freedom to choose the most comfortable screen setting, whatever the situation. While IPX4-rated water resistance adds protection for reading on the go

Under the hood is a Rockchip RK3566 1.8GHz quad-core processor, 1 GB of RAM, and 32GB of internal storage. There is WIFI to connect to the Pocketbook Bookstore or surf the internet. Listen to audiobooks, podcasts, or music with wireless headphones or earbuds via Bluetooth 5.0. It is powered by a 1550 mAh battery, which should last 3 or 4 weeks with light usage.

PocketBook Q gives readers the freedom to build their library without being tied to a single bookstore or content platform. It supports 25 popular ebook formats without conversion, making it easy to enjoy books, comics, and documents from many different sources. Compatibility with Adobe DRM and LCP DRM allows borrowing ebooks from public libraries, including through the pre-installed PocketBook x Libby app. PocketBook Cloud and the PocketBook Reader mobile app keep books, bookmarks, and reading progress synchronized across devices, so every title is always close at hand. This open approach to reading fits naturally with PocketBook Q’s compact, take-anywhere design.

Would you buy the PocketBook Q?

Will you buy the PocketBook Q? If I were a reader looking for a highly portable, phone-sized e-reader, my decision would come down to how I like to manage my digital library. The built-in, native Libby integration is a massive convenience, and PocketBook’s legendary support for 25 different file formats means you rarely have to worry about file conversion. Because it runs on a streamlined Linux system rather than Android, there are no social media apps, email notifications, or web browsing temptations. It is strictly a device for reading. If you prefer tactile page-turn buttons over swiping a small touchscreen, the side buttons on the PocketBook Q are a huge ergonomic win for one-handed reading.

entries.title: Amazon Kindle plastic vs. Kindle with aluminum
entries.summary: Amazon has refreshed its entry-level, 6-inch e-reader lineup by offering two distinct housing options: the standard plastic Kindle and the premium Kindle Aluminum. The post Amazon Kindle plastic vs. Kindle with aluminum first appeared on Good e-Reader.
entries.content:
Amazon’s entry-level 6-inch e-reader lineup offers a unique choice: the standard plastic Kindle and the premium Kindle Aluminum. While both share the same 6-inch, 300 PPI flush-front display, software, and battery life, their exterior designs and bundled features differ completely.

The Kindle (2026) plastic model is highly praised in reviews for its featherlight portability and practical, everyday usability. Weighing just 140 grams, it feels effortlessly comfortable during extended, one-handed reading sessions and delivers a textured, tactile grip that mimics the warm feel of a classic paperback. Reviewers emphasize that while the recycled plastic shell is more prone to minor hairline scratches, it flexes under pressure and survives drops without denting. It serves as the ultimate budget-friendly workhorse, offering the exact same crisp 300 PPI display and software performance as its pricier sibling, making it the smarter value choice for readers who prioritize comfort over premium aesthetics.

Conversely, the Kindle Aluminum shifts the focus toward a luxury experience with several functional hardware upgrades. We appreciate its rigid, matte-finished metal chassis because it eliminates body flex and naturally resists oily fingerprint smudges. Beyond the premium aesthetic, the aluminum version adds practical enhancements reviewers love, including built-in back magnets for snap-on folio covers and accessible external Torx screws that allow easy battery replacement down the road. With 32 GB of storage and an ad-free lock screen out of the box, it is celebrated as gorgeous hardware, though critics often note its higher price tag.

Both of these Kindle models have user-replaceable batteries. Driven by upcoming European Union regulations, Amazon built these models with a removable, user-replaceable back panel (EBR-compliant), entirely shifting away from the tightly glued-shut designs of previous generations. Depending on whether you have a standard plastic model or an upgraded aluminum variant, accessing and swapping the battery differs slightly. Plastic models tend to pop off easily because they have no screws. All you need is your fingernail, a guitar pick, or something similar. Remove the battery by unscrewing the four Phillips-head screws securing it to the frame. On Kindles with an aluminum backplate, remove two tiny hex screws on the bottom edge of the device. Then pry it open with a fingernail, guitar pick, or something similar.

  • The redesigned Kindle — Now thinner, lighter, faster. New edge-to-edge color and a sleeker, 6" front display. Books open 30% faster vs. the previous Kindle.
  • Up to 6 weeks on a single charge — The display only uses power when you turn the page or use the front light.
  • Easy on the eyes — Read comfortably in bright sunlight or at night on a high-contrast, glare-free display with adjustable brightness.

entries.title: What reading benefits does Prime Membership offer?
entries.summary: The Amazon Prime Membership provides access to Prime Reading, Amazon First Reads, and a discounted rate for Amazon Kids+, which has thousands of books and graphic novels. The post What reading benefits does Prime Membership offer? first appeared on Good e-Reader.
entries.content:
An Amazon Prime membership provides fast, free shipping on millions of items along with access to Prime Video, exclusive deals, and member-only savings. However, subscribing also provides a number of reading benefits that most people are not aware of.

Amazon First Reads

Amazon First Reads is a popular, zero-risk perk that allows Prime members to download one free pre-release Kindle e-book each month from a curated list of upcoming titles across various genres. Book reviewers and avid readers praise the program as an excellent, budget-friendly way to discover new authors and explore genres they might not otherwise purchase, especially since any downloaded book is yours to keep permanently. Because it’s included in the cost of an existing Prime membership, it offers an enjoyable, low-stakes routine for book lovers on the first of every month.

However, the general consensus among communities like Reddit and Goodreads is that the monthly selections can be decidedly hit-or-miss. Since the program primarily features titles from Amazon’s own publishing imprints rather than major traditional publishing houses, some readers note that the writing, plot development, and editing quality can feel inconsistent. While it may not consistently deliver mainstream, blockbuster bestsellers, it remains a highly valued benefit for casual readers looking to expand their digital libraries completely free of charge.

Prime Reading

Amazon Prime Reading is an excellent, built-in value perk that gives Prime members free access to a rotating library of several thousand digital books, magazines, comics, and audiobooks. The service is praised as a fantastic cost-saver for casual readers, allowing users to borrow up to 10 titles at a time with no due dates or late fees. Since it is fully included in the standard Amazon Prime subscription at no additional charge, it serves as a zero-risk way to explore new genres and flip through popular monthly magazines right from a smartphone, tablet, or Kindle device.

However, avid readers and book reviewers frequently point out that the service’s limited library and lack of new releases are significant drawbacks. Because Amazon continuously cycles titles in and out of the Prime catalog, readers often find that the selection relies heavily on older bestsellers, short Amazon Original Stories, and lesser-known indie authors rather than the latest blockbuster releases. On platforms like Reddit, users frequently note that voracious bookworms will likely outgrow the small catalog quickly, making a standalone subscription like Kindle Unlimited—which boasts millions of titles—a much better choice for heavy readers despite its added monthly fee.

Amazon Kids+

Amazon Kids+ is widely praised by reviewers as an excellent, cost-effective digital playground for families, offering an expansive, ad-free library of thousands of popular books, movies, TV shows, and educational games from trusted brands like Disney, Nickelodeon, and PBS Kids. Parents highly value the service’s robust, easy-to-use parental controls, which allow them to set strict screen-time limits, filter content by age, and track educational goals through the Amazon Parent Dashboard.

The Amazon Kids+ book library contains thousands of digital books, comics, and graphic novels curated specifically for children aged 3 to 12. Prime Members see a discounted rate of $4.99 per month, instead of $8.99 per month for non-members.
